subject: Streaming architecture

cases.scenario: An export endpoint streams rows from a database cursor as fast as the database produces them. Some clients process rows slowly, and server memory grows until the process is killed.
cases.context: The endpoint has no bounded queue, no credit signal, and no cancellation cleanup when clients disconnect.
cases.question: Diagnose the architecture failure and recommend fixes.
expected_flags: Identifies slow-consumer backpressure as the primary failure.
Names producer, stream, consumer, and where buffering accumulates.
Distinguishes transport-level flow control from an explicit application-level strategy.
expected_fix_hints: Use pull-based reads or a bounded queue that pauses the producer.
Add cancellation handling so abandoned consumers release cursors and buffers.
Load test with deliberately slow consumers and assert memory bounds.
absent_signals: Must not solve this as JSON response-shape design.
Must not assume the database cursor or TCP stack alone bounds application memory.
Must not materialize all rows before streaming.

cases.scenario: A progress stream sometimes goes quiet for 20 seconds during a long compute step. The client treats silence as completion and marks the job done, but the server later emits more progress.
cases.context: The protocol does not send an explicit done event, close frame, trailer, or final chunk marker. Resume state is also unspecified.
cases.question: What is wrong with the stream contract?
expected_flags: Flags that termination must be an explicit signal distinct from quiet.
Explains that reconnect/resume requires a last-seen id or resume token if correctness matters.
Separates liveness/heartbeat from end-of-stream semantics.
expected_fix_hints: Define a `done` event or transport-specific close/trailer semantics.
Add heartbeats only to prove liveness, not to indicate completion.
Include resumable cursor or last-event-id semantics when gaps or duplicates matter.
absent_signals: Must not use timeout silence as completion.
Must not claim SSE-style Last-Event-ID exists for all transports.
Must not ignore partial-result correctness after reconnect.

cases.scenario: A product wants to stream server-generated status updates to a browser. The browser never sends unsolicited messages after connecting, and updates are UTF-8 text events.
cases.context: The team proposes WebSocket because it sounds real time. The infrastructure supports regular HTTP responses more reliably than upgrade connections.
cases.question: How should the streaming-architecture skill frame the transport decision?
expected_flags: Starts from directionality, framing, backpressure, reconnect, and termination requirements.
Recognizes SSE as the simpler default for one-way server-to-client text event streams.
Keeps WebSocket for bidirectional unsolicited messages or binary framed interaction.
expected_fix_hints: Use text/event-stream with explicit event ids if resume matters.
Add an explicit done or terminal event.
Document application-level pacing because SSE has no full application backpressure protocol by itself.
absent_signals: Must not pick WebSocket solely because the feature is live.
Must not treat transport choice as complete without backpressure and termination.
Must not route browser freshness UX concerns to this case unless the low-level stream contract is in scope.

cases.scenario: A React server-rendered route streams partial HTML while data dependencies resolve. A nested boundary fails after earlier chunks have already reached the browser.
cases.context: The team is debating whether streaming means errors can be handled like ordinary all-at-once SSR errors.
cases.question: What should the design account for?
expected_flags: Explains that partial results may already be visible before later work fails.
Names boundary/error semantics as part of the streamed contract.
Connects framework APIs to the underlying producer/stream/consumer/termination model.
expected_fix_hints: Define what fallback or error boundary output can be sent after earlier chunks.
Define abort/cancellation behavior for unfinished rendering.
Verify client behavior for partial output, late errors, and abandoned connections.
absent_signals: Must not treat streaming SSR as identical to a single completed HTML response.
Must not ignore what the consumer has already observed.
Must not collapse this into page-level rendering taxonomy only.

cases.scenario: A team asks for the JSON envelope, status codes, and error fields for a single bounded request/response endpoint.
cases.context: The endpoint returns one complete payload and has no incremental delivery or long-lived consumer.
cases.question: Should streaming-architecture own the task?
expected_flags: Routes the task to api-design.
Explains that streaming-architecture owns multi-value-over-time responses, not single payload shape.
Keeps streaming relevant only if the endpoint later becomes incremental.
expected_fix_hints: Use api-design for payload envelope, status codes, and error shape.
Revisit streaming-architecture only when producer/backpressure/termination questions appear.
absent_signals: Must not force streaming concepts onto a single bounded response.
Must not discuss SSE/WebSocket as the primary answer.

cases.scenario: A dashboard should show when data is stale, reconnect after disconnect, and avoid disruptive auto-refresh while users are reading.
cases.context: The main decisions are freshness indicators, subscription ownership, catch-up behavior, and whether polling/SSE/WebSocket fits the UX.
cases.question: Should streaming-architecture own the task?
expected_flags: Routes browser freshness UX to real-time-updates.
Explains that streaming-architecture owns low-level stream/backpressure/termination contracts.
Notes that streaming-architecture may verify the low-level stream if SSE or WebSocket is selected.
expected_fix_hints: Use real-time-updates for freshness promise, reconnect catch-up, and UI behavior.
Use streaming-architecture only for the underlying producer/consumer/backpressure contract.
absent_signals: Must not treat every SSE/WebSocket question as low-level streaming architecture.
Must not ignore the user-visible freshness contract.

cases.scenario: A CSV export takes 12 minutes and should survive process restarts. The team asks for queue retries, idempotency, and where to persist job status.
cases.context: No incremental stream contract is being designed yet; the work must be durable and retryable.
cases.question: Should streaming-architecture own the primary design?
expected_flags: Routes durable execution, retries, and persisted status to background-jobs.
Explains that streaming-architecture may later deliver progress or results incrementally.
Separates producer execution durability from consumer delivery over time.
expected_fix_hints: Use background-jobs to design queueing, retry, idempotency, and status persistence.
Apply streaming-architecture only to a progress/result stream layered on top.
absent_signals: Must not use a long-lived stream as the durability mechanism.
Must not skip retry and persistence semantics because the output might stream later.
